summary: Lists requirements for making RADIUS crypto-agile, meaning it can switch to stronger cryptography when the old methods weaken. It is a requirements document that lays groundwork for later specifications, and is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: If a lock gets easy to pick, you want to swap it for a better one. This lists what RADIUS would need so its security can be upgraded without starting over.

questions: why is md5 a problem for radius
how does radius stay backward compatible with new crypto
subtitle: What any plan to let RADIUS swap out its aging cryptography has to deliver.

tldr.problem: RADIUS protects packets and hides attributes with MD5-based methods, and MD5's basic cryptographic assumptions are being eroded, but RADIUS has no way to move to other algorithms.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines crypto-agility for RADIUS and lists requirements for any solution: negotiate algorithms, protect against bidding-down, cover every packet type, stay backward compatible, and be interoperable and under IETF change control.
tldr.outcome: It is a requirements document, not a protocol. It sets the bar against which later proposals, first published as Experimental, are judged.

today: RFC 6421 is an Informational requirements document, and its metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It describes what a solution must do and does not define one.

sections.title: Where the Work Came From
sections.content:
The RADEXT working group was asked by members of the Security Area Directorate to prepare a formal crypto-agility work item. The proposal called for reviewing RADIUS against the requirements of RFC 4962, fixing deficiencies in message digest functions, key-wrap functions and the password-hiding function, and defining at least one mandatory-to-implement algorithm in each area.

Because RADIUS is widely deployed and has reached Draft Standard status, the working group adopted a two-phase process. Solutions are first published as Experimental, with a description of implementations and an evaluation against these requirements. The group then selects proposals to advance on the standards track, judged on the requirements, deployment experience and evidence of multiple interoperable implementations.
sections.plainLanguage: People noticed RADIUS's locks were getting old. They decided to write down what a good replacement must do and try ideas on a small scale before making them official.

sections.title: What Crypto-Agility Means
sections.content:
Crypto-agility is the ability of a protocol to adapt to evolving cryptography and security requirements, ideally by updating algorithms without substantial disruption to fielded implementations. For RADIUS it means the ability to automatically negotiate the algorithms used to integrity protect and authenticate packets and to hide attributes. This covers all message types, including Access, Accounting, CoA/Disconnect and Status-Server. Negotiation MAY occur in RADIUS itself or in a lower layer such as the transport.

Proposals MUST NOT introduce generic new capability negotiation or change the RADIUS operational model from RFC 6158. They SHOULD focus on crypto-agility alone and not require new attribute formats.
sections.plainLanguage: Agility means being able to switch to a better lock easily when needed, without replacing the whole door.

sections.title: RADIUS Security Today
sections.content:
RADIUS packets other than Access-Request and Status-Server are protected by an MD5-based integrity check in the Authenticator field, and the Message-Authenticator attribute uses HMAC-MD5. There is no confidentiality for entire packets, though some attributes such as User-Password and Tunnel-Password carry hidden values, using a stream cipher built from an MD5 key stream.

RFC 6151 says advances in MD5 collisions do not immediately compromise MD5 or HMAC-MD5 as used in RADIUS without knowing the shared secret. It also says MD5 must not be used for digital signatures, and that new protocol designs should not employ HMAC-MD5.
sections.plainLanguage: RADIUS uses an old kind of lock. It has not been broken in the way RADIUS uses it, but experts say new designs should not pick it.

sections.title: The Core Requirements
sections.content:
Proposals MUST support negotiating algorithms for per-packet integrity and authentication, provide per-packet replay protection for all message types, and specify mandatory-to-implement algorithms. They MUST avoid security compromise even if existing algorithms or the legacy shared secret are shown to be weak, including protection against bidding-down attacks. Algorithms are RECOMMENDED to be chosen from those classed as Acceptable in NIST SP 800-131A.

  • Confidentiality, by encrypting whole packets or individual attributes, is RECOMMENDED, with negotiable algorithms.
  • Fresh session keys are REQUIRED, and Perfect Forward Secrecy is RECOMMENDED.
  • Support for X.509 certificates is RECOMMENDED, and pre-shared keys SHOULD also be supported.
  • Solutions MUST apply to all RADIUS packet types, and data exchanged with Diameter SHOULD NOT be affected.
  • Solutions MUST be interoperable between independent implementations from the specification alone, and proposals MUST be willing to cede change control to the IETF.
sections.plainLanguage: A good replacement lock must let both sides agree on a strong lock, make new keys often, and stop a trickster from forcing them back to the old lock.

sections.title: Backward Compatibility and Key Management
sections.content:
A solution MUST work with legacy RADIUS clients and servers, but legacy mechanisms are only appropriate before they are compromised. After that, secure algorithms MUST be used. Because RADIUS is request and response, the first request must use predetermined algorithms. One approach secures a request with both legacy and stronger mechanisms, with cryptographically independent credentials. Another probes by omitting legacy protection, which can delay first contact with legacy servers, so upgrading servers first helps.

The RFC concludes automated key management is not inherently required for RADIUS, since it needs O(n) keys and operators already manage shared secrets. But features such as Perfect Forward Secrecy can only come from automated key management, so it is RECOMMENDED, and REQUIRED for modes that need frequent key changes.
sections.plainLanguage: New locks must still open for old keys until the old lock is known to be broken. After that, only the new ones work.
